relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Israel gathers around David with language of shared bone and flesh.
Military leadership and a shepherding oracle become the basis of royal claim.
Elders make covenant and anoint David at Hebron.
The united force moves toward Jebus, a city where people already live.
Jebusite resistance ends in capture and a new royal name for the stronghold.
David offers command to the first attacker, and Joab rises through conquest.
The captured stronghold becomes David's residence and identity.
Royal building expands while Joab repairs the rest of the city.
David's growing power is interpreted as Divine accompaniment.
Warriors and all Israel are credited with establishing his kingdom.
Jashobeam's fame is measured through three hundred deaths.
Eleazar stands among the first three warriors.
A barley field becomes a battleground while civilians flee.
The field and its food are defended through lethal combat.
Three commanders descend toward David while Philistines hold the valley.
Bethlehem, David's remembered home, is occupied by a garrison.
A leader voices a longing that subordinates may hear as a command.
Three men risk their lives for water, and David pours it out rather than consume their danger.
He names the water as their blood, recognizing that desire under power can cost other people their lives.
Abishai's renown is also recorded through three hundred deaths.
Honor is ranked even among the violent elite.
Benaiah's reputation is built through killings of Moabite warriors and a lion.
An Egyptian's unusual height becomes part of a story ending in his death by his own weapon.
Benaiah's deeds create his place among the mighty.
David turns military fame into command of the bodyguard.
The longer roster begins with Asahel and Elhanan.
Shammoth and Helez remain named.
Ira and Abiezer remain named.
Sibbecai and Ilai remain named.
Maharai and Heled remain named.
Ithai and Benaiah remain named.
Hurai and Abiel remain named.
Azmaveth and Eliahba remain named.
Hashem's sons and Jonathan remain named.
Ahiam and Eliphal remain named.
Hepher and Ahijah remain named.
Hezro and Naarai remain named.
Joel and Mibhar remain named.
Zelek the Ammonite and Naharai the Beerothite show a mixed force rather than a pure bloodline.
Ira and Gareb the Ithrites remain named.
Uriah the Hittite appears in the honor roll, and his name accuses the king who arranged his death.
Adina and his Reubenite company are remembered.
Hanan and Joshaphat are remembered.
Uzzia, Shama, and Jeiel are remembered.
Jediael and Joha are remembered.
Eliel, Jeribai, Joshaviah, and Ithmah the Moabite are remembered.
Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel close the warrior list.

contemplative_note: The chapter builds royal greatness from conquest and warrior memory, but its own details resist hero worship. Jebus was inhabited, water cost subordinates mortal risk, foreign-born warriors belonged inside Israel's force, and Uriah's final name keeps royal betrayal from disappearing beneath military glory.
